templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Dash pair around a supplementary element
Colon between independent clauses (second explains first)
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long past-participle opener
items.passage: Since 2015, archaeologists beneath Mexico City have been excavating the Huei Tzompantli, the monumental rack on which the Aztecs publicly exhibited the skulls of sacrificial ______ together with lime mortar into a cylindrical tower adjoining the rack, the skulls number in the hundreds, and some belonged to women and children.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence is complete once it reaches “the skulls of sacrificial captives.” The phrase “Bound together with lime mortar into a cylindrical tower adjoining the rack” describes “the skulls,” the subject of the second main clause, which goes on with the verb “number.” A period between “captives” and “Bound” correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: With no mark, “bound together with lime mortar ...” attaches to “captives,” and the main clause “the skulls number in the hundreds” then follows the first main clause after only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: The comma lets the phrase seem to describe the captives, but the main clause “the skulls number in the hundreds” then follows the first main clause after only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “Who were bound ...” keeps the phrase inside the first sentence as a description of the captives, so “the skulls number in the hundreds” still follows a complete main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: archaeology (Huei Tzompantli, Templo Mayor area, excavated by Mexican archaeologists from 2015; skulls set in lime mortar in a tower, women and children among them). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-7 checks: past-participle opener of 11 words (“Bound together ... adjoining the rack”) that reads naturally on clause 1's last noun (“captives bound”); the comma, glued and who-were options hold until the splice at “the skulls number,” 13 words after the blank; one-sentence run of 48 words; cue outside a 6-word window; reasoning steps 3. Key is not the longest option.
band7_moves: past-participle opener of 11 words that could describe clause 1's last noun (captives bound)
comma, glued and who-were options hold until the splice 13 words after the blank

band7.why: 11-word past-participle opener (“Bound together with lime mortar into a cylindrical tower adjoining the rack”) reads at first on “captives” (“captives bound”); the comma, glued and who-were options hold until “the skulls number,” 13 words on (0fa289a7, a872c60a menu); 48-word run.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before an introductory participial phrase
items.passage: In 1917, Dutch astronomer Adriaan van Maanen photographed the spectrum of a faint white dwarf on a glass plate that subsequently remained in an observatory archive for nearly a ______ the plate in 2016, an astronomer identified absorption lines of calcium, an indication that rocky debris had been accumulating on the star.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1917, Dutch astronomer Adriaan van Maanen photographed the spectrum ... for nearly a century” is a complete sentence. The second sentence opens with the phrase “Reexamining the plate in 2016,” which describes its subject, “an astronomer,” and then gives the verb “identified.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; “an astronomer identified absorption lines of calcium” is a complete clause, so the sentence becomes a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: “And reexamining” has nothing parallel to join in the first clause, and the main clause “an astronomer identified absorption lines of calcium” is still attached to the first main clause by a comma alone.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “reexamining the plate in 2016” runs on from “nearly a century,” and the main clause “an astronomer identified absorption lines of calcium” then follows after only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: astronomy (van Maanen's 1917 plate of the white dwarf now called van Maanen 2, reexamined in 2016 and found to show calcium, the earliest record of a metal-polluted white dwarf). Real subject the writer knows; the 2016 astronomer is left unnamed. No fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape: participial opener of 5 words before clause 2's subject, as in the band-6 models (By dissolving ..., Praising ...). Key is not the longest option.

band7.why: 5-word participial opener before clause 2's subject, as in band-6 aab74a3b and b15724fc; band-6 target, met.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause: semicolon before, comma after
items.passage: Saxaul, a drought-tolerant shrub with extensive roots and nearly leafless branches, is widely cultivated in Central Asia to prevent migrating dunes from burying highways and farmland. The shrubs do not physically obstruct windblown ______ they reduce the wind’s velocity near the ground, so that airborne grains settle and accumulate around their stems.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The shrubs do not physically obstruct windblown sand” and “they reduce the wind’s velocity near the ground ...” are both main clauses, and “rather” introduces the second one as the correction of the first. A semicolon after “sand” joins the clauses, and a comma after “rather” sets off the adverb at the start of the second clause.

B.why_wrong: Commas around “rather” leave two main clauses joined by a comma alone; a conjunctive adverb cannot join clauses the way a conjunction can.

C.why_wrong: Nothing separates the two main clauses, so “The shrubs do not physically obstruct windblown sand rather, they reduce the wind’s velocity ...” runs them together.

D.recipe: misplaced boundary (adverb on the wrong side)
D.why_wrong: The semicolon puts “rather” at the end of the first clause, where it means nothing; “rather” has to open the clause that gives what the shrubs do instead.

items.notes: Subject: ecology (saxaul, Haloxylon, planted to fix dunes in Central Asia; slows near-ground wind so sand settles around it). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape modelled on a9e5b788 (`; rather,` after a negated first clause); options vary the semicolon and comma around the adverb. Key is not the longest option (B and D are as long).

band7.why: “; rather,” after a negated first clause is the band-6 shape (a9e5b788); band 7 never uses rather. Strong band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing the first clause: comma before, semicolon after
items.passage: In the 1100s, German abbess Hildegard of Bingen compiled roughly 1,000 words of a language she called Lingua Ignota (“unknown language”), inventing names for plants, tools, and ecclesiastical officials. She did not construct a complete ______ the vocabulary consists almost entirely of nouns, which she inserted into sentences that otherwise follow Latin grammar.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “She did not construct a complete language” qualifies the first sentence, which says Hildegard compiled “roughly 1,000 words of a language she called Lingua Ignota,” so “however” belongs with that clause and marks the contrast with the sentence before. The next clause, “the vocabulary consists almost entirely of nouns, which she inserted into sentences that otherwise follow Latin grammar,” explains the qualification. A comma before “however” and a semicolon after it join the two main clauses correctly.

A.why_wrong: Putting “however” at the start of the second clause sets “the vocabulary consists almost entirely of nouns ...” against “She did not construct a complete language,” but the second clause supports the first rather than contrasting with it.

C.why_wrong: Commas around “however” leave two main clauses joined by a comma alone.

D.why_wrong: With no mark after “however,” the main clause “the vocabulary consists almost entirely of nouns ...” runs straight on from the first main clause with nothing to join them.

items.notes: Subject: language (Hildegard of Bingen's Lingua Ignota, a glossary of about 1,000 coined words, mostly nouns, used inside Latin sentences such as the antiphon O orzchis Ecclesia). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-7 checks: the adverb closes clause 1, and clause 1 corrects the previous sentence (a 'language' of coined words is not a complete language); clause 2 elaborates clause 1, so the textbook `; however,` fails only on meaning against the previous sentence; cue outside the 6-word window (the contrast is with the first sentence); logic-wrong distractor present. Key is not the longest option.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, which qualifies the previous sentence
logic-wrong `; however,` distractor that fails only on meaning
deciding cue in the previous sentence

band7.why: be37d4ae and c06af4d8 shape and menu. The only contrast is with sentence 1 (“compiled roughly 1,000 words of a language”), which the key's clause-1 “however” expresses; clause 2's main predicate, “consists almost entirely of nouns,” is the reason for “did not construct a complete language,” and “which she inserted into sentences that otherwise follow Latin grammar” also supports it, so no contrastive reading of “; however,” survives for a careful student.

safety.lead_override: 2026-10-27 lead: safety (Opus) chose A '; however,', the band-7 meaning trap. Key B ', however;' is CB's band-7 S1_adverb shape (adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence, as be37d4ae and c06af4d8). In A 'however' would set the nouns-only clause against 'did not construct a complete language', but that clause explains it, so A fails on meaning. Key stands; same call as w4b1_04.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a specifying list
items.passage: Most sundews capture insects on sticky, glue-tipped tentacles, but Drosera glanduligera, a carnivorous plant native to southern Australia, possesses two kinds of ______ glue-tipped ones at the center of each leaf and longer, nonsticky “snap-tentacles” around the perimeter, which can catapult a crawling insect onto the adhesive in a fraction of a second.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “Drosera glanduligera ... possesses two kinds of tentacles” is complete, and what follows names the two kinds: “glue-tipped ones at the center of each leaf and longer, nonsticky ‘snap-tentacles’ around the perimeter.” A colon correctly introduces this list after a complete clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “glue-tipped ones at the center of each leaf and longer ... around the perimeter” has no main verb of its own.

B.why_wrong: The period makes “Glue-tipped ones at the center of each leaf and longer ... second” a sentence of its own, but it is a fragment with no main verb.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “two kinds of tentacles glue-tipped ones at the center ...” runs the list into the clause; a colon is needed to introduce it.

items.notes: Subject: botany (Drosera glanduligera, southern Australia, snap-tentacles at the leaf rim that catapult prey onto the glue tentacles in a fraction of a second). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape modelled on c468db1c (announcing phrase 'two varieties of' then a two-part list; period, semicolon and no-mark distractors). No dash option (a lone dash would be a twin of the colon). All four options are the same length, so check_rw counts the key as longest (a tie).

band7.why: Colon before a two-part specifying list on c468db1c's menu (semicolon, period, no mark); band-6 target, met.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that names what the clause announces
items.passage: Kim Hong-do’s eighteenth-century Album of Genre Paintings holds twenty-five small scenes in ink and light color. Drawn with quick, spare brushstrokes, they depict a subject far removed from the royal court where Kim ______ everyday labor of commoners, among them farmers who thresh rice, roofers who lay tiles, and blacksmiths who hammer iron at a forge.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Drawn with quick, spare brushstrokes, they depict a subject far removed from the royal court where Kim worked” is a complete clause, and what follows names that subject: “the everyday labor of commoners, among them farmers who thresh rice, roofers who lay tiles, and blacksmiths who hammer iron at a forge.” This phrase has no main verb of its own (“thresh,” “lay,” and “hammer” belong to the clauses beginning with “who”), so it can’t stand as a sentence. A colon correctly introduces it after the complete clause.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “the everyday labor of commoners, among them farmers who thresh rice, roofers who lay tiles, and blacksmiths who hammer iron at a forge” is a noun phrase: its verbs “thresh,” “lay,” and “hammer” belong to the clauses beginning with “who.”

C.recipe: added word creates the error (comma splice)
C.why_wrong: Adding “it was” turns what follows into a main clause, so the two main clauses “they depict a subject far removed from the royal court where Kim worked” and “it was the everyday labor of commoners ...” are joined by a comma alone, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: The period makes “The everyday labor of commoners, among them farmers who thresh rice, roofers who lay tiles, and blacksmiths who hammer iron at a forge” a sentence of its own, but it is a fragment: the phrase has no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: art history (Kim Hong-do's late Joseon album Danwon pungsokdo cheop, 25 genre scenes in light color on paper, National Museum of Korea; leaves include rice threshing, roof tiling and a smithy; Kim was a court painter). Replaced in review: the draft's subject, Zhang Zeduan's Qingming scroll, is billed as China's most famous painting and appears in survey textbooks, a topic-fame tell (GENERATE.md). Real subject; no fact-check (WAVE.md); scene list checked against the Wikipedia page for the album. The new passage makes no claim that Kim was first. Band-7 checks: announcing noun phrase with its own relative clause (“a subject far removed from the royal court where Kim worked”); the right side is a noun phrase whose only finite verbs (thresh, lay, hammer) sit inside who clauses, so the semicolon and period look right until the student sees that no main verb follows; comma plus “it was the” splice as in e9aee0d8; run 41 words; cue outside a 6-word window. No lone dash option, no plain comma option (an appositive comma would be a twin). Key is not the longest option.
band7_moves: right side is a noun phrase whose only finite verbs (thresh, lay, hammer) sit in who clauses, so period and semicolon look right
announcing phrase that itself contains a relative clause
comma plus added `it was the` splice; cue more than 6 words from the blank

fixes: replaced the subject (Zhang Zeduan's Qingming scroll, a topic-fame tell) with Kim Hong-do's Album of Genre Paintings, keeping the e9aee0d8 band-7 shape, key letter A and option menu; explanation, why_wrong, notes and band7_moves rewritten; claim appended to claims.txt and the old one withdrawn

band7.why: e9aee0d8 menu: clause 1 ends in an announcing noun phrase holding its own relative clause (“a subject far removed from the royal court where Kim worked”); the right side is a noun phrase whose only finite verbs (“thresh,” “lay,” “hammer”) sit in who clauses 8 to 17 words past the blank, so the semicolon and period look right; comma plus “it was the” splice; no lone dash or plain comma.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive: title and name before the verb, no punctuation
items.passage: Most fashionable European women of the early 1900s wore restrictive corsets beneath their clothing. In 1907, however, Venice-based ______ introduced the Delphos gown, a column of delicately pleated silk that hung from the shoulders and followed the contours of the body without any corset underneath.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Venice-based designer” is a title that describes “Mariano Fortuny,” and the name is essential to the sentence: without it, the reader would not know which designer introduced the gown. No punctuation is used between a title of this kind and the name that follows it, and none is used between the subject “Venice-based designer Mariano Fortuny” and its verb, “introduced.”

A.why_wrong: Setting off “Mariano Fortuny” with commas treats the name as extra information that could be removed, but “In 1907, however, Venice-based designer introduced the Delphos gown” would not say who introduced it; the name is essential, so no commas are used.

B.recipe: comma intrudes into a unit (subject and verb)
B.why_wrong: The comma after “Fortuny” separates the subject “Venice-based designer Mariano Fortuny” from its verb, “introduced.”

D.recipe: comma intrudes into a unit (title and name)
D.why_wrong: The comma separates the title “designer” from the name it identifies, “Mariano Fortuny”; no punctuation belongs between them.

items.notes: Subject: design (Mariano Fortuny's Delphos gown, first made about 1907 in Venice, finely pleated silk hanging from the shoulders and worn without a corset; pleating method patented 1909). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape modelled on 4dcedc31: article-less title + name as the subject, after an introductory “In 1907, however,” that makes commas around the name look natural; four options over the two comma slots. Key is the shortest option.

band7.why: Article-less title + name as subject after “In 1907, however,” (4dcedc31 shape); local cue, band-6 target, met.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction before a second clause that opens with an introductory phrase
items.passage: Scholars disagree by several centuries about the date of the Tolkappiyam, the oldest surviving grammatical treatise in the Tamil language. Its first two books analyze the pronunciation and word formation of the ______ in the third, the treatise turns to literature, establishing conventions for poems about love and warfare.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Its first two books analyze the pronunciation and word formation of the language” and “in the third, the treatise turns to literature ...” are both main clauses. When two main clauses this long are joined in one sentence, a comma goes before the coordinating conjunction: “language, but in the third, the treatise turns ...,” with “but” marking the contrast between the first two books and the third.

A.why_wrong: “But” can join the two main clauses, but when main clauses this long are coordinated, a comma is used before the conjunction.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join two main clauses; “in the third, the treatise turns to literature” is a complete clause, so the result is a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the main clauses “Its first two books analyze ... the language” and “in the third, the treatise turns to literature ...” are fused.

items.notes: Subject: language (the Tolkappiyam, oldest surviving Tamil grammar; its date is disputed by centuries; three books: letters and sounds, words, then subject matter of poetry, including the conventions of love (akam) and war (puram) poems). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Kept off the five-landscape convention, which inferences.S2.hard.w3b2_01 uses. Planned as band 7, but S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/boundaries.md section 5), so written as a strong band 6 with band_target 6 (batch note). Band-6 shape from 59094d87 and 7ce4ee13: the second clause opens with an introductory phrase (“in the third,”), so the comma alone looks like it could do the job. Key is the longest option, as in both models.

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 on 59094d87 and 7ce4ee13 with the intro phrase “in the third,” opening clause 2.

items.subtype: Closing a dash pair around an appositive that contains its own comma
items.passage: In 2009, images from a Japanese lunar orbiter revealed a circular pit roughly 65 meters in diameter in the Moon’s Marius Hills. Many planetary scientists suspect that the pit—a skylight, or collapsed opening in the roof of an ancient lava ______ lead to a cavern spacious enough to protect future astronauts from radiation and micrometeorites.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “pit” opens a supplementary element, “a skylight, or collapsed opening in the roof of an ancient lava tube,” that describes the pit. A second dash after “tube” closes this element, so the sentence goes on with “may lead to a cavern ...,” the verb that belongs to “the pit.” With the element removed, the sentence still reads correctly: “Many planetary scientists suspect that the pit may lead to a cavern ....”

A.why_wrong: A comma can’t close an element that was opened with a dash; the comma after “skylight” belongs inside the element and is not its partner.

B.why_wrong: Without a closing dash, the element opened after “pit” never ends, so “may lead” seems to belong to “lava tube” and the subject “the pit” is left without a verb.

D.why_wrong: Adding “it” gives “may lead” a new subject, so “the pit” is left without a verb and the clause that follows “suspect that” no longer holds together.

items.notes: Subject: planetary science (the Marius Hills hole, about 65 m wide, imaged in 2009 by Japan's lunar orbiter and taken to be a skylight into a lava tube, proposed as shelter for future crews). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). The orbiter is not named, since Kaguya is the probe in official rhetorical_synthesis bc56170b. Band-6 shape: opening dash 12 words before the blank, a comma inside the element (“a skylight, or collapsed opening ...”) that makes a closing comma look like its partner, as the series commas do in aacddbd8. Key is not the longest option.

band7.why: Opening dash 12 words back with a comma inside the element that tempts a comma close (626a1642, aacddbd8); single level, band-6 target, met.

items.subtype: Colon between main clauses; the second opens with a whereas clause and explains the first
items.passage: Uzeyir Hajibeyov’s Leyli and Majnun premiered in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 1908. The opera joins two musical traditions that had seldom ______ whereas the orchestra plays from parts written out in advance in the European manner, the singers improvise long passages within the traditional modes of mugham, a classical vocal art.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The opera joins two musical traditions that had seldom met” is a main clause, and so is what follows it: the subordinate clause “whereas the orchestra plays from parts written out in advance in the European manner” leads into the main clause “the singers improvise long passages ....” The second main clause explains how the two traditions are joined, and a colon is used between main clauses when the second explains the first.

A.why_wrong: The “whereas” clause is followed by the main clause “the singers improvise long passages ...,” so the comma joins two main clauses on its own, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the main clause “The opera joins two musical traditions that had seldom met” runs straight into “whereas ..., the singers improvise ...,” a run-on sentence.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “and” can’t join two main clauses this long, and “and” presents what follows as a separate point rather than as the explanation of how the traditions meet.

items.notes: Subject: music (Hajibeyov's Leyli and Majnun, Baku 1908, the first mugham opera, often called the first opera of the Muslim world: notated orchestral parts beside improvised mugham sections). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-7 checks: clause 1 announces (“joins two musical traditions that had seldom met”); clause 2 opens with a subordinator (“whereas”), so the comma looks legal, and the splice only shows at “the singers improvise,” 17 words after the blank; `and` distractor wrong by relation as well as form (logic tag); run 39 words; reasoning steps 4 (two clause checks, opener of 3+ words, meaning-decided distractor). Key is not the longest option.
band7_moves: clause 2 opens with a whereas clause, so a comma looks legal; the splice shows 17 words after the blank
`and` distractor wrong by relation (logic) as well as form

band7.why: bb4557cf menu and shape: clause 1 announces (“joins two musical traditions that had seldom met”), clause 2 opens with “whereas,” so the comma looks legal until “the singers improvise,” 17 words on; the “and” option fails on relation as well as form.

items.subtype: Comma pair around an interrupting phrase after a conjunction
items.passage: The Kreutz sungrazers are comets whose orbits carry them extraordinarily close to the Sun. Believed to be fragments of a single comet that disintegrated centuries ago, most of them brighten as they approach the ______ vanish entirely, vaporized by its intense heat.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “before reaching it” comes between “and” and “vanish,” the second of the two verbs (“brighten” and “vanish”) that share the subject “most of them.” A supplementary phrase in the middle of a sentence is set off with a pair of commas: one after “and” and one after “it.” With the phrase removed, the sentence still reads correctly: “most of them brighten as they approach the Sun and vanish entirely, vaporized by its intense heat.”

B.why_wrong: The phrase “before reaching it” needs to be set off with paired punctuation; a comma after “and” is needed to match the one after “it.”

C.why_wrong: The comma after “and” opens the phrase “before reaching it,” but nothing closes it; a comma after “it” is needed to match the one after “and.”

D.why_wrong: A single dash after “it” has no partner: no dash after “and” opens the phrase “before reaching it,” so the lone dash only cuts the phrase off from the verb it leads into, “vanish.”

items.notes: Subject: astronomy (Kreutz sungrazing comets, fragments of one parent that broke up centuries ago; most of the small ones found by SOHO evaporate before perihelion). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape modelled on fdb16e20, the only hard S3_comma_pair item (band 6; no band-7 items exist for this template): both commas of the pair sit inside the option, around a phrase after `and`. No option leaves out both commas (that version could be acceptable). Key is the longest option, as in the model.

fixes: reworded the explanation's opening and D's why_wrong (it wrongly called “vanish” the verb of “it”)

band7.why: S3_comma_pair has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 on fdb16e20's exact menu (comma pair after “and,” lone comma, lone opening comma, comma plus dash).

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: The Serat Centhini, a Javanese poem compiled at the royal court of Surakarta in the early 1800s, follows travelers who wander across Java after their homeland is conquered. The plot is ______ the lengthy digressions document Javanese cuisine, music, medicine, and religious ritual in remarkable detail.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The plot is thin” and “the lengthy digressions document Javanese cuisine, music, medicine, and religious ritual in remarkable detail” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them, and “but” marks the contrast between the slight plot and the rich digressions.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the main clauses “The plot is thin” and “the lengthy digressions document ...” are fused.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses “The plot is thin” and “the lengthy digressions document ...,” so the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: The comma belongs before “but,” not after it; “thin but, the lengthy digressions” places the comma between the conjunction and the clause it introduces.

items.notes: Subject: literature (the Serat Centhini, compiled at the Surakarta court from about 1814, an encyclopedic Javanese poem following the wanderings of Sunan Giri's children after the fall of Giri). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Medium shape from a12e3b8a (short first clause, comma-after-conjunction distractor `paradox and,`). Key ties for longest with C.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a short introductory phrase
items.passage: Ennigaldi-Nanna, a Babylonian princess, served as high priestess at the city of Ur around 530 BCE. In the ruins of her residence, archaeologists discovered objects that were already centuries old in her ______ them, they also found clay cylinders that described the objects in three languages, much like modern museum labels.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In the ruins of her residence, archaeologists discovered objects that were already centuries old in her lifetime” is a complete sentence. The next sentence opens with the phrase “Alongside them,” and then gives its subject and verb, “they also found.” A period after “lifetime” correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma lets “alongside them” seem to finish the first clause, but “they also found clay cylinders ...” is a second main clause, and a comma alone can’t join the two.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “alongside them” runs on from “old in her lifetime,” and the main clause “they also found clay cylinders ...” then follows the first main clause after only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “And” could join the two main clauses only with a comma before it; without one, the clauses are joined incorrectly.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Ennigaldi-Nanna, daughter of Nabonidus and priestess at Ur; Woolley's team found older artifacts in her residence with clay cylinder labels in three languages, read as an early museum). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Medium shape: two-word opener (“Alongside them,”) after the period, as in the medium models' two- or three-word openers; an `and` option without its comma as in eef91a50. No `, and` option (it would be a twin). Key is not the longest option.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: In his 1973 film Touki Bouki, about two young lovers in Dakar, Senegal, who dream of emigrating to Paris, director Djibril Diop Mambéty structures the narrative as a series of abrupt, dreamlike ______ unexpectedly from the couple’s motorcycle rides through the city to scenes of cattle in a slaughterhouse.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “director Djibril Diop Mambéty structures the narrative as a series of abrupt, dreamlike fragments” is followed by the participial phrase “cutting unexpectedly from the couple’s motorcycle rides ... to scenes of cattle in a slaughterhouse,” which describes how Mambéty structures it. A comma correctly separates the main clause from this supplementary phrase.

A.why_wrong: The period makes “Cutting unexpectedly ... in a slaughterhouse” a sentence of its own, but this phrase has no subject or main verb, so it is a fragment.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “cutting unexpectedly ... in a slaughterhouse” is a participial phrase, not a main clause.

D.why_wrong: “And” has nothing parallel to join: “structures the narrative ... and cutting” links a main verb to an -ing phrase, which isn’t grammatical.

items.notes: Subject: film (Djibril Diop Mambety's Touki Bouki, 1973: Mory and Anta in Dakar plan to sail to France; elliptical editing, Mory's horned motorcycle, slaughterhouse imagery). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Single long sentence (47 words) so the medium tier keeps CB's sentence length; option set from ac5536c1 with an added-`and` option instead of the bare one. Key is not the longest option.

items.subtype: Closing comma of a nonrestrictive which clause between subject and verb
items.passage: In Kenya, many people save money through chamas, informal groups whose members meet regularly and pool their contributions. A merry-go-round chama, which might consist of a dozen coworkers, neighbors, or ______ gives the pooled money to one member at each meeting until everyone has had a turn.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “chama” opens the supplementary clause “which might consist of a dozen coworkers, neighbors, or relatives.” A second comma after “relatives” closes it, so the sentence goes on with “gives,” the verb for “A merry-go-round chama.” With the clause removed, the sentence still reads correctly: “A merry-go-round chama gives the pooled money to one member ....”

B.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the clause opened by the comma after “chama” never ends, and “gives” seems to belong to “relatives.”

C.why_wrong: A dash can’t close an element that was opened with a comma; a comma is needed to match the one after “chama.”

D.why_wrong: “And gives” makes “gives” part of the which clause, so “A merry-go-round chama” is left without a verb of its own.

items.notes: Subject: economics (Kenyan chamas, informal savings groups; in the merry-go-round type each meeting's pooled contributions go to one member in turn). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). The w3 Words in Context claim on chamas was withdrawn before writing, so the subject is free. Medium shape: opening comma 10 words before the blank, with series commas inside the clause that make the closing comma easy to miss, as in 7f48b098. Key is not the longest option.

items.subtype: Comma after a long introductory participial phrase
items.passage: Shaped like a horn that widens gradually toward the soil’s ______ the underground burrow that a male mole cricket digs amplifies his chirping considerably, allowing the sound to carry far enough to reach females flying overhead on warm evenings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Shaped like a horn that widens gradually toward the soil’s surface” is an introductory participial phrase that describes the sentence’s subject, “the underground burrow.” A comma after an introductory phrase of this kind correctly separates it from the main clause “the underground burrow that a male mole cricket digs amplifies his chirping considerably ....”

A.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “Shaped like a horn that widens gradually toward the soil’s surface” is a participial phrase.

B.why_wrong: Without a comma, nothing marks where the long introductory phrase ends and the main clause begins, so “surface the underground burrow” runs the two together.

D.why_wrong: “And” has nothing to join the participial phrase to; it leaves “Shaped like a horn ...” attached to no subject.

items.notes: Subject: biology (mole crickets sing from burrows whose horn-shaped openings amplify the song; females locate males in flight). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Medium shape: a long introductory participial phrase (11 words, with its own `that` clause) before the subject, as a427a52c and 5cc85f01 put a long phrase before the comma; single sentence for medium sentence length. Key is not the longest option.

items.subtype: Semicolon between independent clauses; the second opens with a short introductory phrase
items.passage: The tenth-century writer al-Hamadhani is credited with inventing the maqama, a short tale told in rhymed Arabic prose. His narrator keeps meeting the same eloquent rogue in different ______ each episode, the rogue talks an audience out of its money and only afterward reveals his identity.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “His narrator keeps meeting the same eloquent rogue in different cities” and “in each episode, the rogue talks an audience out of its money and only afterward reveals his identity” are both main clauses. A semicolon correctly joins two main clauses, and the phrase “in each episode” belongs to the second clause, before its subject, “the rogue.”

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses; “in each episode, the rogue talks an audience out of its money ...” is a complete clause.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “in each episode” attaches to “in different cities,” and the main clause “the rogue talks an audience out of its money ...” then follows the first main clause after only a comma.

C.why_wrong: “And” could join the two main clauses only with a comma before it; without one, the clauses are joined incorrectly.

items.notes: Subject: literature (al-Hamadhani, 968 to 1008, credited with the maqama: rhymed-prose episodes in which the narrator Isa ibn Hisham keeps meeting the rogue Abu al-Fath al-Iskandari, who wins money by eloquence and is recognized at the end). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Medium shape from 4ba99a6f: the second clause opens with a short phrase (“in each episode,”) that can attach to clause 1. No period or `, and` option (they would be twins). Key is not the longest option.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: A Brocken spectre is an optical phenomenon seen by climbers standing between the low sun and a bank of fog. The climber’s shadow, projected onto the fog, can look gigantic, and it is often surrounded ______ concentric rainbow-colored rings known as a glory.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The preposition “by” introduces its object, “concentric rainbow-colored rings known as a glory,” which tells what surrounds the shadow. No punctuation is needed between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, and “it is often surrounded by” is not one; a colon can’t separate the preposition “by” from its object.

C.why_wrong: A dash can’t separate the preposition “by” from its object; nothing in the sentence is being set off.

D.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate the preposition “by” from its object, “concentric rainbow-colored rings known as a glory.”

items.notes: Subject: atmospheric optics (the Brocken spectre, an observer's shadow cast on cloud or fog opposite the sun, often ringed by a glory; named for the Brocken in Germany's Harz mountains). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape: preposition and object, four distinct marks. Key is the shortest option.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: In southern China, the collapse of enormous underground caverns has created tiankeng, sinkholes that can be hundreds of meters deep. Protected by their steep walls from wind and grazing animals, many tiankeng ______ forests that have grown undisturbed for centuries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In the main clause, “forests that have grown undisturbed for centuries” is the direct object of the verb “shelter”: it tells what many tiankeng shelter. No punctuation is needed between a verb and its object.

B.why_wrong: A dash can’t separate the verb “shelter” from its object; nothing in the sentence is being set off.

C.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “many tiankeng shelter” needs its object to be complete, so a colon can’t come between the verb and the object.

D.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate the verb “shelter” from its direct object, “forests that have grown undisturbed for centuries.”

items.notes: Subject: geology and ecology (tiankeng, giant collapse sinkholes in the karst of southern China, some more than 500 m deep, many holding isolated forests on their floors). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape: verb and object after an introductory phrase, four distinct marks. Key is the shortest option.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Sonideros are DJs who set up towering sound systems at neighborhood dances in Mexico City. Between songs, a sonidero often reads out greetings from audience members ______ relatives who have emigrated, many of them to the United States.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The preposition “to” introduces its object, “relatives who have emigrated,” which tells whom the greetings are meant for. No punctuation is needed between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate the preposition “to” from its object, “relatives who have emigrated.”

B.why_wrong: A dash can’t separate the preposition “to” from its object; nothing in the sentence is being set off.

D.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, and “a sonidero often reads out greetings from audience members to” is not one; a colon can’t separate a preposition from its object.

items.notes: Subject: culture and music (sonideros, Mexico City sound-system DJs who read out saludos, dedications that audiences send to family members who have migrated, often to the US). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape: preposition and object, four distinct marks. Key is the shortest option.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: Jazz kissa, cafés where customers listen to recorded jazz, spread across Japan in the 1950s and 1960s, when imported records were too expensive for most fans to buy. Visitors could order coffee or ______ conversation was usually discouraged so that everyone could concentrate on the music.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Visitors could order coffee or tea” and “conversation was usually discouraged so that everyone could concentrate on the music” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them, and “but” marks the contrast between what visitors could do and what was discouraged.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the main clauses “Visitors could order coffee or tea” and “conversation was usually discouraged ...” are fused.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses “Visitors could order coffee or tea” and “conversation was usually discouraged ...,” so the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: When “but” coordinates two main clauses such as these, a comma is conventionally used before it.

items.notes: Subject: culture (jazz kissa, Japanese cafes where patrons listened to the owner's jazz records, common from the 1950s, when imported LPs were costly; many asked for silence). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape and option set from 148be4da. Key is the longest option, as in 148be4da.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: Carved into a marble balustrade in an upper gallery of Istanbul’s Hagia Sophia are fragments of a runic inscription. Although most of the characters have ______ can still identify the name Halfdan, probably that of a Scandinavian who visited the city in the 800s.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Although most of the characters have eroded” is a dependent clause that introduces the main clause “researchers can still identify the name Halfdan ....” A comma correctly separates an introductory dependent clause from the main clause that follows it.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “Although most of the characters have eroded” is a dependent clause.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Although most of the characters have eroded” a sentence of its own, but a clause beginning with “although” can’t stand alone; it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, nothing marks where the introductory clause ends, so the sentence at first reads as if the characters “have eroded researchers.”

items.notes: Subject: history (the Halfdan runes, Norse graffiti on a marble parapet in the upper gallery of Hagia Sophia, usually dated to the 9th century; only the name Halfdan is clearly legible). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Different subject from the live inferences trial item on the building's acoustics. Easy shape from 26c8c88c (Although clause, then the subject inside the option). Key is not the only longest option (A and C are as long).

items.subtype: Embedded question: statement order and a period
items.passage: Lake-effect snow, which forms when frigid air crosses a relatively warm lake, often falls in narrow bands. To warn the right communities, meteorologists analyze wind patterns to determine where ______ Even a slight shift in wind direction can move a band many kilometers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: does the heaviest snow tend to fall?
the heaviest snow tends to fall?
the heaviest snow tends to fall.
does the heaviest snow tend to fall.
items.explanation: The blank completes an embedded question, “where the heaviest snow tends to fall,” which is the object of “determine.” An embedded question uses statement word order (the subject “the heaviest snow,” then the verb “tends”), and because the sentence as a whole is a statement, it ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: Inverted order with “does” and a question mark would suit a direct question, but this clause is part of the statement “meteorologists analyze wind patterns to determine where ...,” so it takes statement order and a period.

B.recipe: question errors (question mark on a statement)
B.why_wrong: The word order is right for an embedded question, but the sentence is a statement, not a question, so it can’t end with a question mark.

D.recipe: question errors (inverted order in an embedded clause)
D.why_wrong: An embedded question doesn’t use inverted order (“does the heaviest snow tend”); the subject comes before the verb: “the heaviest snow tends.”

items.notes: Subject: meteorology (lake-effect snow, cold air over warmer lake water producing narrow, intense snow bands downwind; band position is sensitive to wind direction). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape from aab78b25 (embedded question after an infinitive verb, then a new sentence); 2 x 2 grid of order and end mark, with do-support in the inverted options. Key is not the longest option.

items.subtype: Comma before a sentence-final nonrestrictive which clause
items.passage: The longest known Maya sacbe, or raised road, stretches about 100 kilometers between the ancient cities of Cobá and Yaxuná in Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula. Along its route, archaeologists discovered a massive stone ______ workers may have rolled along the road to flatten its surface.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “Along its route, archaeologists discovered a massive stone cylinder” is followed by “which workers may have rolled along the road to flatten its surface,” a clause that adds information about the cylinder. A comma correctly separates the main clause from this supplementary which clause.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “which workers may have rolled along the road to flatten its surface” is a relative clause, not a main clause.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Which workers may have rolled along the road to flatten its surface” a sentence of its own, but a which clause can’t stand alone; it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: A colon introduces an explanation or a list, not a which clause that describes the noun before it; a comma is used here.

items.notes: Subject: archaeology (Sacbe 1, the Maya causeway of about 100 km from Coba to Yaxuna, built in the early 600s or 700s; a large stone roller found along it is thought to have been used to compact the surface). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape and option set from 667a0587 (`Act, which` with semicolon, period and a fourth mark); no bare option, since `cylinder workers may have rolled` would be an acceptable reduced relative clause. All four options are the same length, so check_rw counts the key as longest (a tie).

items.subtype: Opening comma of a nonrestrictive which clause between subject and verb
items.passage: Matrakçı Nasuh, a sixteenth-century Ottoman mathematician and historian, painted the cities that Sultan Suleiman’s army passed through during a military campaign in the 1530s. His city ______ show buildings, rivers, and gardens in meticulous detail, contain no human figures at all.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “which show buildings, rivers, and gardens in meticulous detail” adds information about “His city views,” and the comma after “detail” closes it. A comma before “which” opens the clause to match, so the sentence still reads correctly without it: “His city views contain no human figures at all.”

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, and “His city views” is only the subject; the clause also needs a comma, not a colon, to match the one after “detail.”

B.why_wrong: Without a comma before “which,” the comma after “detail” has no partner, and it ends up separating the subject “His city views” from its verb, “contain.”

C.why_wrong: The period cuts the subject “His city views” off from its verb, “contain,” so neither “His city views.” nor “Which show ... no human figures at all.” is a complete sentence.

items.notes: Subject: art history (Matrakci Nasuh, Ottoman polymath, whose illustrated account of Suleiman's Iraq campaign of 1533 to 1536 shows the cities on the route without any people). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Replaces the earlier claim on the Royal Game of Ur (withdrawn in claims.txt). Easy shape and option set from ea8f4658, the only easy S3_comma_pair item, with the partner comma 9 words after the blank. All four options are within one character, so check_rw counts the key as longest (a tie).
